1.1 What is assessment?
Assessment is designed to measure what students know, understand and are
able to do. All Huafu International (HFI) subjects are assessed by
coursework (including tests) and examinations (exams). During your
programme you will be given different types of assessment, designed to be
similar to the assessments used at universities.

Assessment (Exams and Coursework)1.1 What is assessment?Assessment is designed to measure what students know, understand and areable to do. All Huafu International (HFI) subjects are assessed bycoursework (including tests) and examinations (exams). During yourprogramme you will be given different types of assessment, designed to besimilar to the assessments used at universities.
Exam and coursework marks are given out of 100. Further information about
the mark and grade system will be given by your tutors.
Huafu International (HFI) will give you a calendar of all tests and
coursework with hand in dates. Teachers will work to ensure the dates are
arranged so that the work is evenly spread through the year.
1.2 How is assessment planned?
Your teachers plan all the assessments at the beginning of the academic
year, in the week before classes start. This information is communicated
with all the other teachers so that they can coordinate their test schedule
and make sure students do not have too many tests in the same week. Your
teachers should give you a general idea of how you will be assessed at the
beginning of the year. This should include test types, number, and
approximate dates. The dates may change, but your teachers should inform
you of this in advance. Teachers have a duty to notify students of the date
of a summative test, or the deadline of a summative assignment, at least
one week in advance.
1.3 What are the rules for coursework?
Different subjects have different assessments, but all subjects follow
these coursework rules:
     All work that you hand in must be entirely your own and written in
      your own words. If your teachers think you have presented someone
      elses work as your own (plagiarism), they will treat the issue very
      seriously and it might result in you receiving no marks for your work
      or you may even be asked to leave the programme. The section on
      Academic Misconduct (cheating) explains this in more detail and you
      can also ask your Huafu International (HFI) tutor.
     If you hand in work late and do not have a valid reason, marks will be
      deducted (taken away). This is explained in more detail below.
     All coursework will be marked (graded) by your teacher and he or she
      will provide some written comments to help you with your learning.
     If you do not pass a piece of assessed coursework, Huafu International
      (HFI) will tell you if you are permitted to resubmit the work. In some
      cases, rules will not allow you to resubmit. Resubmission is at the
      discretion of the teacher. The grade for any resubmitted work will be
      capped at the minimum passing grade, (i.e. 60 for the AP programme).
     You will be given coursework that does not count towards your final
      grade (formative assessments). This coursework an extremely important
      part of your development. It will help you improve your skills in
      particular areas or give you practice for an assessment that does
      count towards your final grade.

different standards for citation of work in your writing. Some may use MLA
while others may use the Harvard system. Check with your teachers which
standards are followed for individual subjects. Although this may seem
inconsistent, it is similar to the experience at university, for which
different subjects and departments will have different regulations.

teacher should give you guidelines on what this means. This is especially

The details of the examinations (exams) for each of your subjects will be
given to you by your tutors. They will also be shown on the academic

1.10 What happens if the rules are broken?
If Huafu International (HFI) suspects that any of the above listed rules
have been broken, Huafu International (HFI) will investigate the matter.
The student(s) concerned will normally be permitted to complete all his/her
exams. Huafu International (HFI) will report the outcome of the
investigation to the Exam Board (see below), which will decide what action
to take. Confirmed cases of serious misconduct will normally result in
failure and exclusion from Huafu International programmes. Students will be
informed in writing of the decision taken by the Exam Board.
1.11 Who will mark my exams and coursework?
Your exams and coursework are marked by the staff at Huafu International
(HFI).
1.12 What is the Exam Board?
The Exam Board is a meeting where students final results are discussed and
confirmed. The main function of the Exam Board is to make final decisions
about marks and grades by considering the views of the members present.
1.13 When do Exam Boards take place?
Internal Exam Boards will take place at the end of each semester.
1.14 What do my results look like?
You will be awarded a mark/grade for each subject you complete, as well as
a grade/letter grade (note: mark is UK English and means the same as
grade in US English; grade in UK English means the same as letter
grade in US English). This mark/grade shows your level of achievement.
1.15 How will I be judged by universities?
Universities will see your grades and letter grades on your official school
transcript.
1.16 When will I receive my results?
Your final results will be available to you within one week of the Internal
Exam Board for semester 2. They will be issued on your end of year reports
(for AP Y10 and Y11 students).

meet with your teacher to discuss the situation. This is usually enough to
resolve the issue, since the teacher can correct any mistakes, or explain
the rubric and results to you.

should contact the relevant head of department (the English department head
for English teachers, the Social Science department head for Social Science
teachers, the Math and Science department head for Math and Science
teachers). This is best done by email. The department head will meet the
teacher to understand the situation, then meet with the teacher and student

Your work will be marked in the same way as all other students on the
programme.

The Centre Principal will consider your circumstance in consultation with
other staff, including your class tutor.
What documentation should I supply?
You will normally need to provide evidence of your disability or condition
e.g. a letter from your doctor.

2. Academic Honesty
Academic honesty is taken very seriously in Western education system. Its
opposite, academic dishonesty (or academic misconduct), is a serious
academic offence. Academic misconduct is where a student does something
dishonest or unacceptable to try and improve his or her marks. Academic
misconduct will result in a penalty (losing marks) and could mean that you
fail the assessment, module or even the programme. For this reason, Huafu
International (HFI) teachers will include training on how to avoid problems
when presenting your work.
2.1 Types of academic misconduct
Academic misconduct can be classified into five types: plagiarism,
collusion, fabrication of results, subcontracting, and examination
misconduct. Each of these is outlined below. The first one, plagiarism, is
by far the most common, and there is therefore more detail for this type of
misconduct. However, all five types are very serious.
1. Plagiarism
   Copying information, thoughts or ideas from a published or unpublished
   source without referencing (showing) where that information, thoughts or
   ideas came from.
     On your programme you will learn how to use sources (e.g. books,
      websites, articles) and reference them properly.
     Huafu International (HFI) may check your work using an online
      plagiarism detection system such as Turnitin.
Plagiarism can be divided into the following types:
     Patchwork plagiarism. Parts of the original author's words are used
      and connected together in a different way, without paraphrase or
      citation. Needs in-text citations and quotation marks added to be
      considered acceptable.
     Stealing an apt term. A short phrase from the original text is used.
      Needs in-text citation and quotation marks added.
     Paraphrase plagiarism. Some of the words and grammar are changed, but
      there are no in-text citations. Needs in-text citations added to be
      considered acceptable.
     Outright copying. Several sentences (or more) are copied directly from
      the source material, without quotation marks and usually without in-
      text citations. Needs paraphrase (and selection), with in-text
      citations added, to be considered acceptable.
2. Collusion
   Where two or more students work together to produce individual
   assessments that contain the same ideas and text.
     It is important that you prevent your work from being seen and used by
      others.
     Even lending coursework to a friend or leaving work on a shared
      computer, not knowing that it will be copied, could result in a
      penalty for collusion. (For example, if it proves difficult to
      establish who copied from whom.)
3. Fabrication of Results
   Where a student presents a set of results that are not from his/her
   observations or calculations, such as in a lab report.
4. Subcontracting
   Where a student employs someone else to write his or her assessment.
5. Examination misconduct
   Where a student seeks to gain unfair advantage in an examination. This
   includes the following.
        Using notes during a test.
        Communicating with someone inside or outside the exam room.

2.2 What are the penalties?
For collusion, fabrication of results, subcontracting and examination
misconduct the coursework assessment or examination mark will usually be
set to zero.
The exception to this is writing before or after a test has finished, for
which the recommended penalty is a 10% reduction in the score.
For plagiarism, the penalty level will depend on whether the level is low
or high.
Low Level Offence
These offenses happen because of inexperience or lack of knowledge of
academic standards. These infringements are likely to involve a small
fraction of the total coursework, are not extensive, and/or occur on a
minor assignment. Stealing an apt phrase and paraphrase plagiarism are the
most common types of low level offence.
Recommended actions for low level offenses are:
        Required meeting with a teacher to discuss academic honesty.
        Resubmission of the assignment, with all instances of plagiarism
         removed.
        Partial or no credit for the resubmitted work [usually resubmitted
         with a late penalty i.e. lose 10% per day]
High Level Offence

nature or which affect a more significant aspect or portion of the

3.1 Attendance policy
It is recognised that in order to succeed in a class, a minimum amount of
attendance is required. At HFI, the normal minimum attendance required of
students is 90%. This is for each course and for each semester. In other
words, students cannot be absent for more than 10% of the course each
semester. This attendance level is for each individual course, not the
programme as a whole. In practice, it is tedious to calculate exact
attendance records for individual classes, because this is affected by days
lost to holidays and other disruptions. An approximation is therefore used
instead. The AP programme is 37 weeks in duration (slightly longer for AP
Y10). It is accepted that around 3 weeks are lost to exams and other
disruptions. This leaves around 34 weeks for teaching and review (for AP).
An AP class which meets five times per week all year therefore has:
       34 x 5 = 170 lessons in total, or 85 lessons per semester.
The total number of lessons a student can be absent for during one semester
is therefore 8.5. The maximum allowable excused absence (rounded up) is set
at 9. More than this (10 excused absences or above) is therefore excessive
and is not permitted.
In order to simplify the calculation for subjects which have different
numbers of hours per week (some classes only meet three or four times a
week, not five), the same maximum figure is used. This is to students
benefit, since technically for these classes, a lower limit should be set.
Absences for double periods (for classes which meet for six periods a week)
are only counted once, since it would be unfair to students who happen to
be ill on, or otherwise miss, a double period day rather than a regular
day.
Note that if you are more than 10 minutes late for a class, or if you leave
a class for more than 10 minutes, you will be marked absent, since you will
have missed too much of the lesson to be classified as present.
Note that attendance rate for pass/fail courses is 80% per semester (lower
than the rate for regular courses). If you fall below this rate, you will
either receive an F grade, or be removed from the course with WP. The
teacher may have additional or more stringent requirements in order for you
to achieve a passing grade in a pass/fail subject. If so, they will inform
you of this at the beginning of the course.

we at HFI understand and recognise that. Six categories of excused absence
have been defined, which should be sufficiently broad to include all types

      leave for SAT)
     university related (e.g. interview)
     summer school (e.g. returning late to school at the beginning of the
      year)
     family emergency

3.3 Excused versus unexcused absence
The school takes unexcused absences very seriously. Repeated instances of
unexcused absence are referred to as truancy or absenteeism, and all
Western schools will have clear policies on how to deal with it. At HFI,
three unexcused absences will take the student to the limit of absences,
and four unexcused absences is considered to be too many.
3.4 Other discipline
In addition to attendance, there are other factors that affect performance
in a class, and which therefore need to be monitored and managed. These
include:
      being in the class on time;
      staying for the whole lesson;
      participating appropriately according to the demands of the teacher;
      attending the correct class.
Attending the correct class means that, for example, if you have English
during period 1, you attend during period 1 and not period 2 or period 3.
Although there may sometimes be reasons why you cannot attend during a
particular period and would like to attend at a different time, the school
has a legal requirement to mark you as absent. This is because the
attendance is an official legal document, which must accurately indicate
whether or not you were present at the specified time. This would be
important, for example, if you were implicated in a crime.
Wearing the appropriate uniform is also important. Students are expected to
wear appropriate uniform at all times during the school day, both in and
out of class.

absent, late) will be entered by the teacher. Administrative staff will
update the attendance records on submission of a leave request form (see
Appendix 5) to show these as excused absence, if the absence is approved.

HFI recognizes that many students wish to attend a summer school programme.
Students are not encouraged to miss any school time to attend such
programmes, and a calendar is issued very early (usually in January) for
appropriate planning. However, they may be exceptional occasions when
students need to miss one or more days at the start of the academic year
because of summer school participation. In this case, you must notify the
Principal directly before mid-May. Notification must include full and clear
documentation of the reason for arriving late, including:
     exact dates of summer school;
     date you will be coming back to HFI (you must arrive back at school as

You must contact teachers of your courses prior to leaving school for the
summer to be clear on summer assignments and other work.
You must complete the summer assignment for each class and send to teachers
one week before the start of the school year. Teachers may also assign

5.1 Promotion to next grade level
In order to be promoted to the next grade level, you must pass a majority
of your classes. In practice, this means the following.
     You can fail a maximum of 2 subjects in total.

If you fail more courses than the maximums above, you will not be able to

5.2 Course replacement policy
Failed courses can have a major impact on your college application. To help
mitigate this, HFI has a course replacement policy. The policy is that if

the course will be the only ones which will show, whether higher or lower.
Note that this policy only applies if it is possible for you to repeat the
class. It is not possible, for example, to repeat grade 10 classes in grade

Appendix 3: GPA Calculation
What is the GPA?
GPA, short for Grade Point Average, is an average of your grades. However,
it is not a simple average, because it depends on many things: the number
of hours for each course (which determines the course credits), and the
difficulty of each course (which determines which scale is used to
calculate the GPA). The GPA is usually a number between 2 and 5, and uses a
different scale from your other grades.
Why is it important?
The most important part of your college application is your grades. This
does not mean your GPA. It means the grades between 0 and 100 that teachers
give you for each of your subjects. The GPA is important as it gives a
snapshot view of your grades. College tutors might look at it for a very
general idea of your study. They will, however, do this in conjunction with
other scores on your transcript.
How is it calculated?
There are two important concepts to understand how your GPA is calculated.
   1) The weighting scale. Unlike your grades, your GPA does not use a 100
      point scale. Instead, it uses a points scale, so grades on a 100-point
      scale need to be converted to points scale. The table on the next page
      shows how this is done. Typically schools use 4-point scale for
      regular courses, 4.5-point scale for Honors courses, and 5-point scale
      for advanced courses (such as AP) or accelerated courses. HFI uses a 5-
      point scale for all courses. This is because all courses are either
      advanced or accelerated.
   2) Course credits. The average used to calculate your GPA is not a
      simple mean. Instead, it is a weighted average, based on number of
      credits. The credit value of a course is related to number of hours a
      course has over the whole year. Typically, a course which is 4 or 5
      hours a week for two semesters will have 1.0 credit, while one
      semester courses have 0.5 credits. Pass/fail courses, although they
      give credit shown on the transcript, are not included in the weighted
      GPA.
The formula for calculating the GPA is as follows. There is an example on
the next page to help you understand.
    (course credit x GPA contribution) / total course credits

Using a planner will help you to organize your time better, and therefore
help you to improve your grades and reduce your stress.
Tips for Using a Planner
     Make the planner a part of your daily routine. Remember to check it
      every morning and every night.
     Fill in your assignment due dates as soon as you learn them. Get in
      the habit of writing in your planner while you're still in the
      classroom.
     Add reminders. When you write a due date in your planner, go back a
      day or a week and give yourself a reminder that the due date is
      approaching.
     Break down tasks and use backward planning. If you have a research
      paper to write, dont just put the due date. Add the date you will
      begin researching, when you will work on the first draft, etc.
     Use a color-coding system. For example, you could put assignment due
      dates in one colour, college interviews in another colour. You could
      also colour code different subjects. This is especially useful for
      visual learners.
Things to Include in Your Planner
It is important to block off anything that consumes your time, in order to
avoid conflict and crisis. You should include:

     Test dates

     External test dates such as SAT, ACT or TOEFL
